newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto was first woman premier of an Islamic state.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto was first woman premier of an Islamic state.

text.p: Benazir Bhutto, who is seeking to regain power in Pakistan that she has twice won and lost, is a political battler who became the first woman to head a government in a modern Islamic state.
Her name Benazir means "unique" -- and Bhutto is unique in being the only woman to reach the pinnacle of power in Pakistan and the only prime minister to give birth while in office.
The charismatic daughter of Pakistan's first popularly elected leader, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, Benazir has seen her family stalked by tragedy.
Her father was hanged in 1979 by the military government which had ousted him and both her brothers were killed in mysterious circumstances.

A gritty fighter who thrives on adversity, the largely Western-educated Bhutto is battling against the odds to win Monday's elections, smarting from her unceremonious dismissal by President Farooq Leghari, a former ally.

She had hoped that the Supreme Court would reinstate her, but the court ruled last week that there was enough evidence of corruption, nepotism and other abuses to justify Leghari's action in sacking her three-year-old government.

Conventional wisdom says Sharif will ride to victory on a tide of public anger at the alleged corruption and misrule that marked Bhutto's administration, but some voters may recall that his last government was sacked on the same grounds.

"The people of Pakistan will vote for a courageous leadership which brought an end to terrorism in Karachi," Bhutto declared at a rally on Saturday, a reference to the port city where ethnic and faction fighting and battles with security forces cost about 500 lives last year.
A PPP spokesman dismissed as "rubbish" a Sunday Times report that she might be persuaded to take refuge in Britain if she lost the election to avoid a sensitive corruption trial.
The paper quoted Pakistani government sources as saying charges against Bhutto and her jailed husband, Asif Ali Zardari, would be dropped if she left the country and abandoned politics.
Zardari is held on a charge of conspiring in the murder of his wife's brother Murtaza, shot dead by Karachi police in unexplained circumstances in September. He denies the charge.
In a new twist to the political feuding within the Bhutto clan, Ghinwa Bhutto, Murtaza's Lebanese-born widow, has taken on the leadership of her husband's breakaway faction of the PPP.
Zardari, who was investment minister in his wife's cabinet, is seen as her biggest liability and prime target of an anti-corruption drive launched by the caretaker government.
Benazir has tried to divert attention from her spouse's alleged misdeeds by turning her guns on Leghari.
"I was elected by the people of Pakistan and not by one man, but I have been dismissed by one man and not the people of Pakistan," Bhutto said, demanding that Leghari resign.
While in power, Bhutto had sworn to ride out the political and economic storms battering her government and seek a fresh mandate at elections she said would be held in October 1998.
She portrayed herself abroad as a woman struggling against the odds to steer her turbulent Islamic country on a moderate course of economic liberalisation and social justice.

Bhutto, a mother of three and an inveterate traveller, impressed foreign audiences, but economic and security problems -- notably a long-running conflict with the ethnic Mohajir National Movement in Karachi -- dented her popularity at home.

She gave short shrift to political foes, pursuing corruption cases against former prime minister Nawaz Sharif and his family in the courts and virtually banning coverage in the state media of cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan.
Bhutto took over the PPP after her father was hanged in 1979 on the orders of former military ruler General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq, who had toppled him in 1977.
For 11 years she fought vainly against Zia. Bhutto and her mother Nusrat were often in prison or under house arrest.
In August 1988 Zia died in a mystery air crash. Bhutto, weak from the birth of her first son, took to the hustings and the magic of the Bhutto name proved as potent as ever.
Her 1988 election victory was welcomed worldwide as the advent of democracy in Pakistan after more than a decade of military rule.
President Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her after just 20 months, accusing her of presiding over large-scale corruption.
She clawed her way back to power in the October 1993 election after three years in the political wilderness, only to be sacked a second time by a different president.
Bhutto, who wears an Islamic-style scarf on her head, was born on June 21, 1953, in Karachi, the first of four children.
She was educated at a Christian mission school in Karachi, Radcliffe (now part of Harvard) University, and Britain, where she became president of the Oxford Union debating society.
